speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- JOB-CREATION PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in the debate today on the motion introduced by the official opposition. Yesterday, we commemorated in this House the second anniversary of our return to office. This day brings back to me the rout of the Progressive Conservative Party at that time. When I heard those who spoke today, first the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), then his colleague from Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty) and, finally, my good friend from Joliette (Mr. La Salle), I said to myself that they were still in a rout. Firstly, their motion is taken directly from a letter written by some Liberal colleagues. Their speeches were almost entirely made up of quotations from Liberal colleagues throughout the country, and everything we heard concerned the Liberal Party. This means, Mr. Speaker, that the official opposition should thank the Canadian people for re-electing us two years ago, because they had nothing to say. The members opposite have gone to the trouble of having a motion put on the Order Paper on behalf of the official opposition so they could speak only about the Liberals. Have we heard any valid solutions today? Have we heard any suggestions? None whatsoever, Mr. Speaker. In the minutes at my disposal, I would like to ask them why they did not take any action in certain areas since they would like the population to believe that they could have done so. It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that our government, and especially the Department of Employment and Immigration, have taken and will take action to respond to the present economic situation.
We shall have to face some very important issues in the next few years and we shall have to do what is needed to meet the demand, as concerns both the economy and manpower. Yesterday I read an article in the Montreal Gazette about a confer-

February 19, 1982
Supply
ence arranged by the Financial Post and dealing with future technologies. This article pointed out how essential it was for Canada to plan a major catch-up operation in this field. In fact, most other industrialized countries do face the same problem. However, in the case of Canada, at a time when our traditional sources of immigration are becoming more and more depleted and we are considering extensive industrial megaprojects, it is obvious that we have to make additional, and especially concentrated efforts on a national scale.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the importance of the challenge which we shall be facing during the forthcoming decade in the human resources field has been described in various studies mentioned by the minister this morning, and more specifically in that sponsored by our own department and conducted under the leadership of one of our colleagues and dealing with employment prospects for the eighties. In the past 12 months, Mr. Speaker, the government, the private sector and the trade unions have become very concerned with human resources policies. The consultations which led to the recent federal-provincial conference held in Vancouver early in January to deal with job training are now over and we are about to implement a most effective training program for the whole country. This will be a flexible program which will meet today's needs and provide long-term benefit to all Canadians. We are now witnessing a dramatic decrease in supply throughout the country. The average growth rate of the labour force, which had reached 3.5 per cent in the early sixties and seventies, will have fallen to a mere 1.8 per cent by the end of the eighties. In addition, the make-up of the labour force will have undergone radical changes. The number of newcomers on the labour market will decrease during the next decade and two thirds of them will be women. In western Canada the native people will account for over 20 per cent of the population increase. At least one out of every five newcomers on the labour force will be from the native community in that part of Canada. The average age of the workers will substantially increase. This factor alone will affect the labour market and even our daily life.
Mr. Speaker, all members are well aware of the unprecedented changes that will occur in the economy and the labour market during this decade. However, we are faced with an extraordinary paradox. The unemployment figures are high, but the evolution of our economy is causing serious manpower shortages, especially in the specialized fields. In fact, certain jobs cannot be filled in Canada because of a lack of specialized workers, and this is why we have to call on immigrants to fill certain positions.
No later than this week, the president of a big engineering firm in Montreal pointed out, and rightly so, that the country is very short of engineers at this time, and that this shortage will become crucial in the years to come; that it may even
harm the megaprojects we are planning to get under way. Similarly in private industries, Mr. De Grandpre, chairman of Northern Telecom spoke recently of the shortage of qualifications in his own company. He predicts that Northern Telecom will have to recruit up to 65,000 engineers and experts over the next ten years, if it wants to keep and strengthen its lead in the key technological fields of electronics and telecommunications. A study of those needs in manpower, and especially skilled labour, and the high rate of unemployment, makes action imperative. There is a pressing need to speed up the process of change in the training system across the land. That is precisely why we had that great conference in early January where the topic of vocational training was debated at length.
Like all my colleagues in the House I witnessed the general outcry on the part of certain provinces which were accusing us of trying to interfere in a field of provincial jurisdiction. Of course they did not take into account the fact that our purpose was to train people who are already out of the education system and on the labour market. We also noticed that the province of Quebec was reluctant to participate in this program. Last year we gave the province of Quebec about $65 million for vocational training.
Mr. Speaker, I was very surprised today when I heard the arguments of our colleagues opposite because they did not even say that those programs exist in the province of Quebec. My colleague from Joliette did say that the members from the province of Quebec were not doing anything in the House of Commons. I would like to remind him that during the constitutional debate the Leader of the Opposition and a few of his colleagues tried to bring pressure to bear on the government of Quebec in an attempt to make certain amendments to our constitutional proposal. Mr. Speaker, they knew full well that it was a sheer waste of time to try to convince an openly separatist party to sit at the bargaining table in Ottawa with a view to amending a proposed constitution. They knew beforehand that it was an exercise in futility.
But in concrete cases such as this vocational training project, where do our friends opposite stand? Did they try again to pressure the Quebec government to sit at the same table with us in an effort to renegotiate that constitutional agreement? Did they? I would like to know. I hope that our friend from Joliette who is telling us that he is just- I am looking forward to the reaction of the Quebec government in that respect to see if indeed they will be able to convince the Quebec government.
We on this side of the House have offered to the government of Quebec a program especially designed to train throughout Canada the skilled labour force we will need to meet our needs in the coming years.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) has just announced another very important program, a program he successfully negotiated with the government of Ontario to enable roughly 2,000 forest workers to be
February 19, 1982

actively employed during the short period until they go back to their regular jobs this spring. Under this program, the provinces and Ottawa can sign agreements based on the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act, Section 38, which makes it possible to set funds aside for keeping the most severely affected workers gainfully employed.
In addition to their regular work, these workers can make a useful contribution to their community while collecting additional unemployment benefits. In Ontario, the provincial government has contributed up to $60 a week to the salary of these workers in addition to implementing and administering the program. 1 hope the Conservative friends will help us convince the provincial government to sign these agreements. I am informed that the Quebec government will submit proposals shortly, and I hope that our friends of the Conservative Party, as well as those to my far right, will support the signing of such agreements with the Quebec government in order to keep those Canadians at work.
Mr. Speaker, before going back to the subject of training, I would like to say a few words about the announcement made on December 22 by the Minister of Employment and Immigration concerning a very important program which will provide another $50 million for job creation. A significant part of those $50 million was intended for work sharing. Indeed, under that formula, as of February 16 the Canadian government had earmarked $5 million to help thousands of Canadians workers. Almost 68 agreements have been signed across the land, of which four only in Quebec, and we hope businessmen in my province may take advantage of this program to the same extent as those in other provinces. Under those agreements already reached, 4,144 employees agreed to share the work available with 1,903 others of their colleagues who otherwise would have been laid off. There again, funds are taken from unemployment insurance money as a contribution that almost makes up the money paid for days that are not worked. This keeps more people at work and skilled workers in the industry and certainly helps raise the spirits of those workers.
Mr. Speaker, company presidents told us last week that thanks to that extremely significant program, it had been possible to keep people at work in some industries, so that they can fulfil contracts they may now sign and will be able to sign in one or two months down the road. This program introduced by this government will enable those workers to keep their jobs on a permanent basis, which is quite different from the suggestion heard earlier that we were putting money into temporary jobs exclusively.
I would now like, Mr. Speaker, to come back to what I said earlier and outline the purpose of that famous legislation the Minister of Employment and Immigration will be introducing next spring for manpower training. Since the Adult Vocational Training Act was passed, the federal government has been much involved in institutional training programs which en-
Supply
abled a good number of Canadians to acquire high and medium skilled training. However, that kind of training no longer meets existing market requirements. In the future, adult retraining programs will not be implemented in isolation. Vocational training courses will be more closely related to manpower requirements and the regional and national labour markets. There is no social or economic justice in training Canadians for job opportunities which do not exist.
The government intends to increase its purchase of training units in the specialized trades of national dimension which do not require previous training, such as draftmen and computer programmers, and in the training programs. We intend to focus our efforts on the trades of national dimension and the other labour intensive trades. We intend also to create a professional adaptation and development fund, to provide the necessary sums to build or update training facilities. These facilities, which will be found throughout Canada in the areas where they are needed most, will help people who are compelled to leave their jobs because of the technological revolution, in a quickly changing world, obtain the necessary training to secure employment in other highly specialized trades.
In the area of in-industry training, it is also essential to increase our financial contribution and to gear more precisely the federal government's effort to the trades where the need for specialized workers is greater. The program will be an essential part of the new in-industry program, the purpose of which is to develop the capacity to train 10,000 highly specialized workers every year. Its priority will be to help Canadian workers whose jobs are threatened by the technological revolution.
Both in the in-industry training program and the on-site training programs, women and other disadvantaged groups will be assured of equal opportunities. We shall provide employers with incentives to assist them in training or retraining underprivileged groups and increasing women's training opportunities in traditional occupations. To this end Mr. Speaker, at the Vancouver conference most provincial and the federal governments unanimously decided to urge industry to work in collaboration with the federal and provincial governments toward the setting up of training facilities which are so urgently needed for our manpower. Obviously, industries will benefit from those training opportunities because they will be able, as was indicated earlier, to respond to the technological revolution and rapidly changing working conditions.
To be efficient, any new training system should be flexible enough to adjust in medium and long runs, to imbalances between supply of and demand for highly specialized professions and trades. Most people agree that the present analysis method has been and still is woefully inadequate. Therefore, they proposed the introduction of a system of skilled labour requirement projections in Canada which is the best means available to ascertain the demand levels, over a period of three

February 19, 1982
Supply
to ten years, in such professions that require nine months or more of training. The new system will be sufficiently accommodating to allow for the exercise of judgment.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- JOB-CREATION PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for providing me with the opportunity to speak in support of the motion that has been presented to the House by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). The motion contains not only a substantial part dealing with the matter of job creation in Canada now, but it also supports the principles of parliamentary democracy upon which our whole Canadian system is based. I will explain that in a moment.
First let me say what we are trying to do and what the Leader of the Opposition is trying to bring to the attention of the House and the Canadian public is the fact that ten Members of Parliament on the government side have stood up to be counted on the issue of the budget and the tremendously adverse effect it is having on the Canadian economy and, more important, on the Canadian people. That is what this motion is all about. We in the opposition want to band together with those members on the government side who stood up to be counted on this issue. We want to support them. We want them to know that we are here to help them because we are all here to help the people of Canada.
We cannot help the people of Canada if we back off to a government which insists on putting in proposals and programs against the wishes of the people of Canada. That is why the motion involves parliamentary democracy.
We were sent here by people in constituencies right across Canada, in the provinces of Quebec, Nova Scotia and British Columbia, to represent them. That is what we must do. That is our purpose for being here. That is what the members who signed that letter, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), the Minister of State (Mr. Joyal) and the eight private members who joined together did to make this presentation and proposal.
They are saying to the government and to the people of Canada that they know what Canadians need and want is jobs. They have to go to work. What are we talking about when we talk about unemployment in Canada? We talk about the 1.2 million people officially unemployed in Canada, according to government statistics.
It is worse than that. It has been mentioned several times in this House and other places that those statistics are not accurate. There are many more people unemployed in Canada. Statistics Canada surveys simply scratch the surface. They take into account those people out of work and looking for jobs, of which there are 1.2 million. Unfortunately, there are millions of others in much similar circumstances. There are those who have given up looking for a job. There are at least
250,000	who know that they cannot find work in Canada, no
matter how they look. They are in provinces such as Newfoundland.
If you speak to the provincial authorities there, they will tell you that the unemployment rate there, which is officially close to 20 per cent, is even higher because so many people have given up looking for a job. They know they cannot get work.
It is the same in the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, and I believe all across Canada. There are thousands of Canadians who have given up looking for work. Therefore, it is not just the 1.2 million who are officially unemployed. There are those who know they cannot get jobs and have given up.
It is even worse than that. It is not only those 1.2 million Canadians. There are an additional 1.5 million Canadians with part-time jobs. What are part-time jobs? That is working less than 30 hours a week. Who wants to work less than 30 hours a week? You cannot support yourself and a family with the most menial tasks or low-paying jobs. If you work less than that, you are in poverty. There are 1.5 million of these persons in Canada. The unfortunate part is that 70 per cent of them are women. In many cases these women have to work to support a family. Either their husband has deserted them, they are widowed or they have to provide for themselves. 1 repeat, 70 per cent of the 1.5 million persons in Canada in that situation are women.
In addition, there are another 250,000 persons who are underemployed. These are people with qualifications for higher level jobs, but they cannot get those jobs. There are teachers working as waitresses in restaurants in order to maintain themselves. There are thousands of them across Canada amounting to a total of 260,000 persons in this situation. People with Master's degrees are working in the post office as mail sorters. You see this everywhere you go.
When you add up all those figures and talk about unemployed persons in Canada, you cannot just take the 1.2 million who are officially unemployed. You have to include the 1.5 million who are in part-time jobs, the 250,000 who have given up looking for jobs and the 260,000 who are unemployed. That comes to a grand total of almost three million Canadians in a situation where they either do not have any work, have given up looking for work, have a part-time job, or are employed at menial tasks much below their qualifications. That is over 10 per cent of the total population. That is the situation in Canada.
The Prime Minister wonders why members from Quebec get together to consider the matter, draw up a letter and send it to him saying, "Mr. Prime Minister, for heaven's sakes, create some jobs in Canada. We have almost three million people either out of work, underemployed, looking for work or giving up and becoming destitute." They are saying that something has to be done. It is as simple as that. We are responding to it. We have a motion before the House supporting those people. We want to know what other members of the government will do about this motion. Will they realize, as did their colleagues who signed this letter, that the situation has gone beyond
February 19, 1982

acceptability to Canadians and support their colleagues? We have to join together and take steps to rectify this.
What will we do about it? The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) supposedly answered the problems of Canada when he introduced his budget on November 12. Did it create jobs or economic programs or a climate which would lead to industrial expansion? No, it went to the other extreme. It provided a great number of disincentives. The solution provided in the budget was to tax the working people more. The Minister of Finance, in his budget, told business that it was gypping the tax man and he would set new rules. The government will move in and examine the businesses and discourage them from further expansion or development. That is the solution to the problem which exists in Canada which was given by the Minister of Finance.
You have to wonder what motivates the minister. Is he blind? Does he never return to his constituency? Do you know what the situation is like in his constituency of Cape Breton Highlands-Canso, Mr. Speaker? There is a post office on every corner and parks everywhere. His constituents need the parks because there are no jobs and there is nothing else to do. The minister never provided any jobs in his constituency. The minister provides $2 million, twice a year, toward winter works and student work programs in his constituency. Every other constituency in Nova Scotia receives $100,000 for the same kind of projects. That is how he treats his constituents. The Strait of Canso has the deepest and best port on the Atlantic coast, but there is nothing there. There used to be an oil refinery there, but it has closed down. The common-user dock has been virtually unused. But the Minister of Finance gives them post offices, parks and little projects. That is how he deals with unemployment in his constituency.
Now, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) charges him with the responsibility of dealing with unemployment all across Canada. That surely gives us an indication of the difficulty we are in. The Minister of Finance does not understand the situation. The Peter Principle has set in. He has gone beyond the level of his own competence.
Fortunately, there are members of his own party who realize this problem. Not only do members of the opposition parties, the national press, or most of the economists recognize this, members of his own party realize that he does not know what he is talking about.
The minister has lost control and has brought in insufficient measures to revive the economy. Worst of all, he is misleading Canadians as to what he is doing. The minister has introduced these budgetary provisions and has attempted to tell Parliament and the people of Canada that he is practising restraint. He says that he will cut down on the federal deficit, but he is not fooling the Economic Council of Canada. It realizes that it is not cutting the federal deficit but simply transferring it to the provinces. He is merely flowing the $5 billion from the federal deficit into the provinces. This deficit will be on their books because it is money which comes from transfer pay-
Supply
ments and payments from established programs. The minister has done nothing about government spending.
The proof magically appeared before me today. I saw an announcement in the Ottawa paper today that the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) and the Prime Minister were announcing the construction of a new national museum at a cost of $185 million. The government will spend $185 million on a museum! Earlier today we heard the minister for housing (Mr. Cosgrove) say that he was implementing programs to assist Canadians in their housing needs. The provisions in the budget were to help home owners in dire straits and provide $7,500 per unit for 15,000 units to help people who want to rent houses. The implementation of the proposals which are provided in a bill which he has before the House will cost a total of $350 million. While the government is providing $350 million to help those Canadians with excessive mortgage interest rates and those who need rental accommodation, at a time when occupancy is unavailable in most Canadian cities, it will spend $185 million on a museum. I think Canada's heritage is important, but we must not have home owners losing their homes through foreclosure and have all those social problems which would result. We cannot have Canadians who cannot afford rental accommodation forced to the streets to seek assistance from municipalities while the government builds a museum for $185 million. Where is the heart and soul of the government?
The minister does not understand the needs of Canadians. Why do the Liberal Members of Parliament, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance not travel across Canada to find out what the needs of Canadians are? Have they closed their eyes? They developed a budget which they thought would bring equity into the tax system.
If the government wanted to bring equity to the tax system, they would have conducted a proper investigation and listened to the problems Canadians have with the tax system. They have discussed these problems in order to develop a tax system which would be fair to all Canadians.
When the Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker formed the Government of Canada he set up the Carter commission to examine the tax system. It travelled across Canada to discuss Canadians' problems and ultimately came up with proposals for a change in the tax system. These proposals were contained in the Carter commission report. That is the method for bringing equity into a tax system.
However, when the Carter commission report was introduced in 1967, Mr. Bud Olson, who is now a senator and minister of the Crown, stood up and said that "Liberal MPs rejected the Carter tax reform after years of study." Mr. Olson said that he and his colleagues in the Liberal Party totally rejected tax reform. That was in 1967.
Since that time, there has been a Liberal government in Ottawa, except for a short period, which has done nothing about tax reform. The government has never consulted the people of Canada. On November 12, the government produced a document which it said would bring equity to the tax system. The government never indicated that there was not equity in

February 19, 1982
Supply
the tax system or who was complaining about it. It just took it upon itself to remedy the whole system.
The equity which it claims to have achieved is accomplished by reaching out to 13 million insurance policy holders who are trying to provide for their families and taxing the benefits under that protection. Canadians buy insurance to protect their families, not to cheat the tax man. There are seven million Canadians who participate in health and dental plans, and the government says that it will tax them and make them pay. It does not care what happens to their children's teeth or if they get adequate medical care. All the government wants is dollars.
The government is correct about one matter. The only resource in this country is the people of Canada. They are the only ones who will pay tax. The oil will stay in the ground, the coal will stay in the mines and the wheat will stay in the fields unless Canadians turn it into wealth. The government is trying to tax that wealth. It is trying to tax the work of the Canadian people, but they have caught on and will not stand for it.
The Minister of Finance has been exposed and everyone knows that he has no knowledge of the tax system. We all know he knows about managing government expenditures. The Minister of Finance is making up for years of extravagant spending. Now he has to go to Canadians and take away the pensioners' $1,000 deductions. Fie does not care about the business people or insurance companies, they can provide for themselves, but he will tax the seven million workers in the housing construction industry. He will tax transportation for salesmen. How can this help the people of Canada?
The government reaches out to Canadians and attempts to tell them it is bringing equity to the tax system. No one believes that, including their own members. That is why we have put it in a resolution before the House.
Hon. members opposite had better stand up and vote properly because the people of Canada will be watching. They will know what hon. members opposite are doing. The people know what they are saying at home. It is in the newspapers. It is on the record. We are putting it on the record here. Hon. members opposite must realize and recognize that they are going to be counted. The jig is up. Never mind the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister. Hon. members opposite are on their own now. The Prime Minister cannot protect them. There is no problem in Mount Royal. Everybody is happy there. The problems are in Amqui, Quebec and in the Matapedia Valley where people are out of work and starving to death.

speechtext:
The only reason this government is able to introduce this budget is that hon. members to my left in the New Democratic Party stood up and voted against my party when it was in government. That government was prepared to introduce proper economic measures which were responsible. Members of the New Democratic Party are not off the hook. They are part and parcel-someone said the New Democratic
Party is the Liberal party west. The Liberals have no representation from the west, so they haul in a few members of this red rump and bring them into their plans. If members of the New Democratic Party really wanted to defeat the government and if they really were upset with the tax measures in the budget, as we are, they could have voted the government out last Friday. Instead, they got together and called the whole thing off. They want to stay here. I do not blame them. They will never be any more comfortable than they are now because it is going to get worse for them from here on. The people of Canada are on to them. They know what is going on.
As I said, it is every man for himself on the government side. Hon. members opposite must stand up and be counted. The Prime Minister cannot help them. The Minister of Finance cannot help them because he is in trouble himself. The people in his constituency are sick of post offices, parks and little job-creation programs. They want the Strait of Canso developed. They want the oil refinery opened. They do not want the little bits and pieces of things the minister has been sending down. People are sick of this situation. They want Canada to go ahead and be developed, and they want the government to bring in proposals which would allow for that development. They are sick of the present policies. They are sick of being fooled. We have exploded the myth, and now hon. members opposite are going to have to live with it.
I want to end on a positive note. I admire those members of Parliament in the Liberal Party who got together and said, "This is what has to be done, Mr. Prime Minister; this is what you have to do to correct the situation in Canada; we have to have job-creation programs". Young people are out of work. We need jobs for our young people. We have to protect unemployed persons. We have to bring them back into the labour force so that they can provide for their families. If the government does not do that, we will have social disorder in Canada. Everyone is pointing that out. A psychiatrist in my constituency has written an article in which he points out very graphically the ill effects of unemployment and that lack of security for families and people generally leads to all kinds of social ills. We cannot sit here in Parliament with a blind eye to that kind of problem. We have to do something about it, and we have to do something about it now, not next week and not in the next budget. We must do something right now, and hon. members opposite know that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- JOB-CREATION PROGRAMS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- JOB-CREATION PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say just one more thing. As representatives of the people in Parliament, we are often asked what our role is here. What is our role here? There was a famous parliamentarian, Edmund Burke, who said he was a delegate of the people. When he was elected to Parliament, he made up his mind and decided what to do. Edmund Burke was elected to Parliament in 1774 from the city of Bristol. At that time people were illiterate. They did not know how to handle national affairs. That is not the situation in Canada today. We do not need any Edmund Burkes. We do not need anyone here passing his opinion on what we should be doing. We want

people here who respond to the needs, the wishes and problems of the people of Canada. We are here to represent the people of Canada. I am here to represent the people of Halifax West. The Prime Minister is here to represent the town of Mount Royal. Perhaps the people in the town of Mount Royal do not have problems, but I can tell hon. members that there are problems in Halifax West, in Amqui, in the Matapedia Valley, in Gaspe and all across Canada. The problem is lack of economic activity and unemployment. That is the problem. We need job-creation programs to solve that problem, and that is why we have introduced this motion. That is why we have to stand up and vote on this motion. That is why we are calling upon hon. members opposite to join with us and to forget about the Prime Minister and the town of Mount Royal. Let them forget about that area of Montreal and its mansions, its houses and imported cars. Let them think about the northern regions of Quebec. Let them think about the Gaspe and why a train has to be stopped in the Matapedia Valley to draw attention to these problems.
